title: More than all (Luke 20:41–21:4)
hook: beware showy religion; the widow gave out of her poverty

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sadducees' trick question, children of the resurrection, and a God of the living. Your line was all live to him. Whose name did you say out loud? Day five hundred seventy-four.

A hospital lobby, and a donation wall. Big brass plaques for the biggest gifts, smaller ones below, a long list of names in tiny print at the bottom. In the temple courts in Jerusalem, Jesus looks up and sees the rich putting their gifts into the treasury. Their gifts are large. He's just finished warning the crowd about religion that wants to be seen. And then a poor widow walks up and drops in two mites, tiny coins. On a plaque, her name wouldn't make the list. Jesus says something that rearranges the whole wall.

First the warning, in the King James words: "Beware of the scribes, which desire to walk in long robes, and love greetings in the markets, and the highest seats in the synagogues, and the chief rooms at feasts." He's not attacking scribes as a group. Yesterday some of them told him he'd spoken well. He's describing a kind of faith that wants an audience, and he adds a harder line: they "devour widows' houses, and for a shew make long prayers." Then, straight after, a widow. Her two coins were lepta, from a Greek word meaning small, or thin. Luke has Jesus say: "Of a truth I say unto you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all: For all these have of their abundance cast in unto the offerings of God: but she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had." More than they all. The gift is measured by what's left over afterward, and she has nothing left. Readers take this in two ways, and both are in the text. The familiar reading hears praise: total trust, giving from what you'd rather keep. Some scholars notice where Luke put it, right after the warning about leaders who swallow up widows' houses, and hear a lament too: a system that takes a poor woman's last coins. Either way, Jesus saw her, and Luke makes sure we do too.
screen: then, large: `ALL THE LIVING THAT SHE HAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give where no one will see. Settle, and breathe. Think of one gift you could give this week that no one would ever thank you for. Money, quietly, to someone in need. An hour of help, unannounced. A kind word about someone, said where they'll never hear it. Notice any wish to be seen giving it, without guilt. Then choose one, and picture doing it with no plaque and no audience. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
Lepta. The tiny coins, worth almost nothing, that a poor widow drops into the temple treasury, a gift Jesus says is worth more than all the rich gave.

Your line: out of her poverty. This week ran from Zacchaeus's open door to ten pounds, shouting stones, tears over a city, a beloved son, the God of the living, and now two coins. Today, give one quiet gift that costs you something. Day five hundred seventy-four, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: The phrase the widow's mite comes from the King James wording of this story, and churches read it when inviting people to give, to charity or to the church, quietly and in proportion to what they have.

fork.setup: you're with Jesus in the temple court, watching the gifts go in. the rich give large sums; a widow drops in two tiny coins. who gave the most?
fork.reveal: "this poor widow hath cast in more than they all": she gave all the living that she had.

original.note: Greek: small, thin. also the name of a tiny coin, the mite of the King James Bible; the widow gave two.

trapdoor: what you thought: be generous like the nice old lady.
what it means: a gift is weighed by what's left after it. she gave all she had to live on, and Jesus saw her.
what a scholar hears: Luke sets her right after 'which devour widows' houses', so some read the scene as lament over a system as well as praise of her trust.

notes: The carry says 'poverty'; the KJV of Luke 21:4 reads 'penury'. Both mean the same here.
The lament reading of the widow's offering is associated with Addison G. Wright (1982) and others; presented as a minority reading alongside the common one. Confirm fairness.
Lepton: the smallest coin in circulation; Greek leptos, 'small, thin'. Confirm.
Luke 20:41–44 (David's son question) is in the reading but not taught, to keep one idea. Consider whether a mention is needed.
